assertion: encore — An encore is an additional performance given after the scheduled programme has ended.
crowd surfing — During crowd surfing, audience members pass a person overhead from hand to hand.
soundcheck — A soundcheck tests the venue sound system and adjusts levels before the audience arrives.
set list — A set list records the planned running order of songs for a performance.
supporting act — A supporting act performs an earlier, usually shorter set before the headliner.
Queen — Queen released We Will Rock You on the 1977 album News of the World.
Neil Diamond — Neil Diamond wrote and recorded Sweet Caroline, which became a crowd singalong at many sporting events.
Liverpool FC — Liverpool supporters adopted You’ll Never Walk Alone in the 1960s and still sing it before matches.
the White Stripes — The White Stripes released Seven Nation Army in 2003, and its riff became a worldwide sports chant.
Gala — Gala Rizzatto released Freed from Desire in 1996, and its melody later became a popular football chant.
Abbey Road — The Beatles were photographed on the crossing outside their London studio for the Abbey Road cover.
Nirvana — Nirvana used the underwater baby photograph for the cover of its 1991 album Nevermind.
David Bowie — Brian Duffy photographed David Bowie in the lightning-bolt makeup created for the Aladdin Sane cover.
Andy Warhol — Andy Warhol supplied the banana artwork and was credited as the album producer.
Unknown Pleasures — The Unknown Pleasures cover visualises radio pulses recorded from pulsar CP 1919.
saxophone — The saxophone has a conical metal body but produces sound with a single reed like a clarinet.
bagpipes — Bagpipes feed stored air from a bag into a melody pipe and one or more drone pipes.
kazoo — A kazoo uses a vibrating membrane to colour the sound of a player humming into it.
steelpan — A steelpan has tuned note areas hammered into the surface of a steel drum.
theremin — A theremin senses hand position around its antennas to control pitch and volume.
reggae — Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s from ska, rocksteady, and other influences.
tango — Tango emerged in working-class districts around Buenos Aires and Montevideo.
mariachi — Modern mariachi groups combine strings and trumpets and are strongly associated with Mexican celebrations.
fado — Fado became established in Lisbon and is commonly accompanied by Portuguese guitar.
calypso — Calypso singers use memorable melodies and wordplay to comment on public events and society.
Destiny’s Child — Beyoncé rose to fame as a member of Destiny’s Child before releasing solo albums.
Phil Collins — Phil Collins joined Genesis as drummer and took over lead vocals after Peter Gabriel left.
Lady Gaga — Stefani Joanne Angelina Germanotta adopted Lady Gaga as her professional name.
Freddie Mercury — Farrokh Bulsara adopted the name Freddie Mercury while building his career with Queen.
Elton John — The British singer and pianist legally changed his name to Elton Hercules John.
Ludwig van Beethoven — Beethoven’s Bagatelle No. 25 in A minor is widely known by its dedication Für Elise.
The Nutcracker — Tchaikovsky included the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy in the second act of The Nutcracker.
Richard Wagner — Wagner wrote the Bridal Chorus for his opera Lohengrin.
Also sprach Zarathustra — Stanley Kubrick used the opening fanfare of Also sprach Zarathustra in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Carl Orff — Carl Orff set the medieval poem O Fortuna to music in his cantata Carmina Burana.
the Battle of Waterloo — ABBA’s song compares a romantic surrender with Napoleon’s defeat at Waterloo.
Wayne’s World — The car singalong in Wayne’s World helped return Bohemian Rhapsody to the charts.
Deep Purple — Deep Purple wrote Smoke on the Water after seeing smoke spread over Lake Geneva from the Montreux Casino fire.
2001: A Space Odyssey — Bowie’s title was a play on 2001: A Space Odyssey, which he saw before writing the song.
Francisco Tárrega — The familiar Nokia tune comes from a phrase in Tárrega’s 1902 guitar piece Gran Vals.
Dolly Parton — Dolly Parton wrote and recorded Jolene, whose narrator fears losing her partner to another woman.

assertion: drumstick — A drumstick is a specialised beater used to strike drums, cymbals and other percussion instruments.
fret — A fret is a raised strip on the neck of a stringed instrument that helps set the vibrating length of a stopped string.
a piano pedal — Piano pedals are foot-operated levers that alter the instrument's sound, for example by sustaining notes or making them softer.
a capo — A capo clamps across a fretted instrument's strings to raise their pitch while the player uses familiar chord shapes.
rosin — Rosin is rubbed onto bow hair to create the friction needed to set a string vibrating.
the Moonlight Sonata — Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 is commonly known as the Moonlight Sonata, a nickname added after his death.
Chopsticks — Chopsticks is a widely known piano waltz played with the hands vertical and the little fingers making a chopping motion.
The Entertainer — The Entertainer is a rag by Scott Joplin that gained renewed popularity through the film The Sting.
Clair de lune — Clair de lune, whose title means moonlight, is the third movement of Claude Debussy's Suite bergamasque.

assertion: Frère Jacques — Frère Jacques is a traditional French round about a sleeping friar.
Kalinka — Kalinka is a Russian song written by Ivan Larionov; its title refers to the guelder-rose or snowball-tree plant.
Auld Lang Syne — Auld Lang Syne is a Scots-language song traditionally sung around the world at the close of the old year.
Guantanamera — Guantanamera is a Cuban song whose Spanish title means a woman from Guantánamo.
Danny Boy — Danny Boy sets words by Frederic Weatherly to the traditional Irish melody Londonderry Air.
a jazz trio — A jazz trio is a three-musician ensemble, often formed by piano, double bass and drums.
swing music — Swing music became a dominant popular jazz style in the 1930s through dance-oriented big bands and bandleaders such as Benny Goodman.
ragtime — Ragtime is a strongly syncopated musical style that became widely known through published piano music and player-piano rolls.
walking bass — Walking bass creates regular movement through a mostly stepwise or arpeggiated line that outlines the harmony.
cool jazz — Cool jazz developed after the Second World War with a comparatively relaxed and restrained approach.
a bass drum — A bass drum is a large low-pitched drum used to provide a deep beat in ensembles including marching bands.
a snare drum — A snare drum has wires called snares stretched beneath its lower head, producing a sharp rattling sound.
a bugle — A bugle is a simple brass signal instrument that normally has no valves; the player's embouchure controls its notes.
sousaphone — A sousaphone is a tuba designed to coil around the player, making it practical for marching and outdoor performance.
a euphonium — The euphonium is a low-sounding valved instrument, and marching models have a horizontal, forward-facing bell.
a musical staff — A musical staff is a set of usually five horizontal lines with spaces between them, used to write notes.
a bar line — A bar line is a vertical mark in notation that shows the boundary between measures.
a quarter note — A quarter note has a filled notehead and a stem and normally receives one beat in 4/4 time.
a repeat sign — A repeat sign marks music that should be performed again, usually with dots beside paired vertical strokes.

assertion: a time signature — A time signature indicates how many beats are grouped in each measure and which note value represents a beat.
Peter and the Wolf — Sergei Prokofiev wrote Peter and the Wolf as a narrated orchestral tale in which instruments represent the characters.
The Carnival of the Animals — Camille Saint-Saëns's suite The Carnival of the Animals portrays a playful procession of animals in separate movements.

supportingSource.title: The Carnival of the Animals — Wikipedia

assertion: The Sorcerer's Apprentice — Paul Dukas composed The Sorcerer's Apprentice in 1897, and the piece became widely known through Disney's Fantasia.
Peer Gynt — Edvard Grieg composed incidental music for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, including Morning Mood and In the Hall of the Mountain King.
William Tell Overture — Rossini's William Tell Overture opens the opera about the Swiss hero, and its galloping finale became famous as the theme for The Lone Ranger.
yodeling — Yodeling features rapid repeated changes between the lower chest register and the higher head register.
sea shanty — A sea shanty is a rhythmic work song formerly sung aboard large sailing vessels to coordinate labour.
doo-wop — Doo-wop is a rhythm-and-blues vocal style known for close harmony and repeated nonsense syllables.
barbershop music — Barbershop music uses close four-part unaccompanied vocal harmony, traditionally labelled lead, tenor, baritone and bass.
the whistle register — The whistle register is the highest register of the human voice and produces very high, flute-like tones.
Bruce Springsteen — New Jersey singer-songwriter Bruce Springsteen wrote and recorded Born in the U.S.A. and is widely nicknamed The Boss.
Billy Joel — American singer-songwriter Billy Joel wrote Piano Man after working as a lounge pianist in Los Angeles.
Tracy Chapman — American singer-songwriter Tracy Chapman wrote Fast Car and Talkin' 'bout a Revolution for her self-titled debut album.
James Taylor — American singer-songwriter James Taylor wrote and recorded Fire and Rain for his album Sweet Baby James.
Carole King — Carole King co-wrote Will You Love Me Tomorrow before becoming a recording artist and songwriter behind the album Tapestry.
electronic drums — Electronic drums use playable pads and an electronic sound module to produce percussion sounds.
MIDI keyboard — A MIDI keyboard is a piano-style controller that sends MIDI performance data to another device or software instrument.
a loop station — A loop station records short passages and repeats them so a performer can build layered music live.
a digital audio workstation — DAW software is used to record, edit, arrange and mix digital audio.
music sequencer — A music sequencer records, edits and plays back musical performance information in an ordered sequence.
Latin pop — Latin pop is a broad label for popular music from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking areas and performers.
mambo — Mambo is a Cuban dance-music genre that Pérez Prado popularised internationally in a big-band form.
Latin jazz — Latin jazz combines jazz with Latin American rhythms, especially through Afro-Cuban and Afro-Brazilian branches.
rock en español — Rock en español is the Spanish-language term for rock music performed with Spanish vocals.
son cubano — Son cubano developed in eastern Cuba by combining Spanish-derived song and guitar with African-rooted rhythms, vocal exchange and percussion.
Andrea Bocelli — Blind Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli became internationally known through recordings that cross between classical and popular music, including Time to Say Goodbye.
André Rieu — Dutch violinist André Rieu founded and leads the Johann Strauss Orchestra, known for popular performances of waltzes.
Yo-Yo Ma — Cellist Yo-Yo Ma has recorded Bach and founded the Silk Road Ensemble alongside his classical career.
Maria Callas — Greek-American soprano Maria Callas was one of the twentieth century's most renowned opera singers and was nicknamed La Divina.
Lang Lang — Chinese concert pianist Lang Lang, whose two names have the same Latin-alphabet spelling but different tones, performed at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games opening ceremony.
tap dance — Tap dance uses shoes fitted with metal taps to create rhythmic percussion through footwork.
Charleston — The Charleston is an energetic dance named for Charleston, South Carolina, and closely associated with the 1920s.
foxtrot — The foxtrot is a smooth progressive partner dance commonly taught with a slow-slow-quick-quick rhythm.
cakewalk — The cakewalk developed as a competitive dance whose prize was often a cake, and its name later became a term for something easily accomplished.
shimmy — The shimmy is a dance in which the body is held fairly still while the shoulders move rapidly back and forth.
K-pop — K-pop is South Korean popular music that gained a large international audience through acts including BTS and BLACKPINK.
J-pop — J-pop is the common abbreviated name for modern Japanese popular music.
Hindi film music — Hindi film music consists of songs written and performed for Hindi-language cinema and is widely associated with Bollywood.
Afrobeats — Afrobeats is an umbrella term for contemporary West African popular music, distinct from the older genre called Afrobeat.
Cantopop — Cantopop is a form of popular music associated with Hong Kong and sung chiefly in Cantonese.
Frédéric Chopin — Frédéric Chopin was a Polish-born Romantic composer and pianist celebrated for works including nocturnes, études and mazurkas.
Franz Liszt — Hungarian Romantic composer and pianist Franz Liszt wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies and many virtuoso piano works.
Franz Schubert — Viennese composer Franz Schubert wrote the art song Erlkönig and the work known as the Unfinished Symphony.
Johannes Brahms — German Romantic composer Johannes Brahms wrote four symphonies and the collection of Hungarian Dances.
Felix Mendelssohn — German Romantic composer Felix Mendelssohn wrote the Wedding March as part of his music for A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Rammstein — Rammstein is a German industrial-metal band known for Du hast and concert performances featuring extensive pyrotechnics.
The Cardigans — The Cardigans are a Swedish rock band fronted by Nina Persson and known for songs including Lovefool and My Favourite Game.
Foo Fighters — Dave Grohl founded the American rock band Foo Fighters after his time as Nirvana's drummer.
Nickelback — Nickelback are a Canadian rock band fronted by Chad Kroeger whose breakthrough international hit was How You Remind Me.
Muse — Muse are a British rock trio fronted by Matt Bellamy and known for songs including Supermassive Black Hole and Uprising.
Graceland — Paul Simon began “Graceland” by recording in Johannesburg with South African musicians, a decision that also provoked controversy over the anti-apartheid cultural boycott.
Exile on Main St. — Much of “Exile on Main St.” was recorded with the Rolling Stones Mobile Studio at Villa Nellcôte in southern France.
OK Computer — Radiohead recorded most of “OK Computer” at St Catherine’s Court, a historic mansion owned by Jane Seymour, using their own equipment.
Buena Vista Social Club — Ry Cooder produced “Buena Vista Social Club” during a short 1996 session at Havana’s EGREM studios with veteran Cuban performers.
The Basement Tapes — Recordings made by Bob Dylan and the Band at the house known as Big Pink in 1967 were later compiled for the official album “The Basement Tapes”.
Motown — Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit; the company marketed its polished soul recordings as “The Sound of Young America”.
Sun Records — Sam Phillips founded Sun Records in Memphis; its early roster included Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins and Jerry Lee Lewis.
Stax Records — Stax Records built its Memphis soul sound around an integrated group of studio musicians including Booker T. & the M.G.’s.
Factory Records — Factory Records was the Manchester independent label behind Joy Division and New Order; its unusually broad FAC catalogue also numbered objects and events.
ECM Records — Manfred Eicher founded ECM Records in Munich in 1969; the label became known for a distinctive spacious sound and minimalist presentation.
(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life — Bill Medley and Jennifer Warnes recorded “(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life” for “Dirty Dancing”, where it accompanies the final dance.

supportingSource.title: (I've Had) The Time of My Life — Wikipedia

assertion: You Never Can Tell — Quentin Tarantino used Chuck Berry’s “You Never Can Tell” for Vincent and Mia’s dance-contest scene in “Pulp Fiction”.
Stuck in the Middle with You — “Reservoir Dogs” famously contrasts the violence of Mr Blonde’s warehouse scene with Stealers Wheel’s “Stuck in the Middle with You”.

supportingSource.title: Stuck in the Middle with You — Wikipedia

assertion: Lust for Life — Iggy Pop’s “Lust for Life” plays over the opening chase and narration of “Trainspotting” and became closely associated with the film.

supportingSource.title: Lust for Life (Iggy Pop song) — Wikipedia

assertion: The End — Francis Ford Coppola used the Doors’ “The End” over the opening montage of “Apocalypse Now”.
Songs of Innocence — Apple distributed U2’s “Songs of Innocence” automatically to iTunes accounts in 2014, prompting complaints from users who had not requested it.
Biophilia — Björk released “Biophilia” as a multimedia project whose songs were accompanied by interactive apps.
The Life of Pablo — Kanye West continued updating “The Life of Pablo” after its initial digital release, treating the album as an evolving work.
Zaireeka — The Flaming Lips designed “Zaireeka” as four synchronized CDs that listeners play at the same time on separate sound systems.
Once Upon a Time in Shaolin — Wu-Tang Clan created one physical copy of “Once Upon a Time in Shaolin” and sold it through a private auction.

supportingSource.title: Once Upon a Time in Shaolin — Wikipedia

assertion: While My Guitar Gently Weeps — Eric Clapton played lead guitar on the Beatles’ “While My Guitar Gently Weeps”, though he was not credited on the original album.

supportingSource.title: While My Guitar Gently Weeps — Wikipedia

assertion: Beat It — Eddie Van Halen played the guitar solo on Michael Jackson’s “Beat It” and did the session without payment.
Layla — Duane Allman contributed prominent slide guitar to Derek and the Dominos’ recording of “Layla”, alongside Eric Clapton.
You’re So Vain — Mick Jagger contributed uncredited backing vocals to Carly Simon’s “You’re So Vain”.
Fame — David Bowie wrote “Fame” with Carlos Alomar and John Lennon; Lennon also played guitar and supplied backing vocals.
Video Killed the Radio Star — MTV launched on 1 August 1981 by showing the Buggles’ “Video Killed the Radio Star” as its first music video.

supportingSource.title: Video Killed the Radio Star — Wikipedia

assertion: Daisy Bell — Bell Labs researchers programmed an IBM 7090 to sing “Daisy Bell” in 1961, an early demonstration of computer speech synthesis.
Switched-On Bach — Wendy Carlos recorded “Switched-On Bach” on a Moog synthesizer; the bestselling album helped bring the instrument to a mass audience.
O Superman — Laurie Anderson built “O Superman” around a repeated vocal pulse, electronic processing and a message framed like an answering-machine recording.
Rockit — Herbie Hancock’s “Rockit” prominently featured GrandMixer DXT’s scratching and became a mainstream showcase for turntablism.
Blackstar — David Bowie released “Blackstar” on 8 January 2016, his 69th birthday; he died two days later.
(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay — Otis Redding recorded “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay” shortly before his death; it was completed and released posthumously.

supportingSource.title: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay — Wikipedia

assertion: The Show Must Go On — Brian May wrote “The Show Must Go On” while Freddie Mercury was seriously ill; Mercury nevertheless recorded its demanding lead vocal.

supportingSource.title: The Show Must Go On (Queen song) — Wikipedia

assertion: You Want It Darker — Leonard Cohen released “You Want It Darker” in October 2016, shortly before his death; cantor Gideon Zelermyer and the Shaar Hashomayim Choir appear on the album.
American IV: The Man Comes Around — Johnny Cash’s “American IV: The Man Comes Around”, produced by Rick Rubin, includes his acclaimed cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Hurt”.

supportingSource.title: American IV: The Man Comes Around — Wikipedia

assertion: Don’t You (Forget About Me) — “Don’t You (Forget About Me)” was offered to several performers before Simple Minds agreed to record it for “The Breakfast Club”.
Can’t Get You Out of My Head — Cathy Dennis and Rob Davis wrote “Can’t Get You Out of My Head”; it was offered elsewhere before Kylie Minogue recorded it.

supportingSource.title: Can't Get You Out of My Head — Wikipedia

assertion: Telephone — Lady Gaga originally wrote “Telephone” for Britney Spears before recording the song herself with Beyoncé.
Rock Your Body — The Neptunes originally offered “Rock Your Body” to Michael Jackson before Justin Timberlake recorded it.
How Will I Know — George Merrill and Shannon Rubicam wrote “How Will I Know” with Janet Jackson in mind; Whitney Houston ultimately recorded it.
Live at the Apollo — James Brown recorded “Live at the Apollo” in 1962 and personally financed it after King Records initially opposed a live album.

supportingSource.title: Live at the Apollo (1963 album) — Wikipedia

assertion: At Fillmore East — The Allman Brothers Band recorded “At Fillmore East” at New York’s Fillmore East in March 1971; it became the group’s breakthrough release.
Cheap Trick at Budokan — “Cheap Trick at Budokan” was first intended for Japan; strong import demand led to a US release and the band’s breakthrough.
Jazz at Massey Hall — “Jazz at Massey Hall” documents a 1953 Toronto concert by a quintet of leading bebop musicians including Parker and Gillespie.

Sunday at the Village Vanguard — For “Sunday at the Village Vanguard”, Evans and Keepnews chose tracks that showcased LaFaro, including two of his compositions; other performances from the same sessions became “Waltz for Debby”.

supportingSource.title: Sunday at the Village Vanguard — Wikipedia

assertion: Ode to Joy — The Council of Europe and European Union use the “Ode to Joy” theme from Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony as their anthem, in an instrumental arrangement.
Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 — Elgar’s “Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1” supplied the melody of “Land of Hope and Glory” and became associated with graduations in the United States.
Finlandia — Finlandia grew from Sibelius’s 1899 press-celebration music. Its hymn-like section later received Finnish lyrics and gained a separate patriotic life.

assertion: Zadok the Priest — Handel composed “Zadok the Priest” for George II’s 1727 coronation; it has been performed at every British coronation since.

Fanfare for the Common Man — Aaron Copland wrote “Fanfare for the Common Man” in 1942 for Eugene Goossens’s wartime fanfare project, taking its title from Henry Wallace’s “century of the common man” speech.

supportingSource.title: Fanfare for the Common Man — Wikipedia

assertion: Cats — Andrew Lloyd Webber based “Cats” on T. S. Eliot’s “Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats”, setting much of the poetry to music.
Les Misérables — The musical “Les Misérables” adapts Victor Hugo’s 1862 novel about Jean Valjean and revolutionary Paris.
Billy Elliot the Musical — “Billy Elliot the Musical”, with music by Elton John, is adapted from the 2000 film “Billy Elliot”.
Evil Dead: The Musical — “Evil Dead: The Musical” is a rock musical based on Sam Raimi’s Evil Dead franchise; its first act adapts “The Evil Dead” and its second act “Evil Dead II”.
Once — The stage musical “Once” adapts the 2007 Irish film and uses songs by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová.
Summertime — “Summertime” originated as an aria in Gershwin’s opera “Porgy and Bess” and was later recorded extensively by jazz musicians.
My Favorite Things — Rodgers and Hammerstein wrote “My Favorite Things” for “The Sound of Music”; John Coltrane’s extended jazz version became one of his signature recordings.
Mack the Knife — “Mack the Knife” originated in Brecht and Weill’s “The Threepenny Opera” and later became a pop and jazz standard.
Autumn Leaves — Joseph Kosma composed “Les Feuilles mortes”; Johnny Mercer later wrote the English lyrics for the standard known as “Autumn Leaves”.
Nature Boy — eden ahbez wrote “Nature Boy” and brought it to Nat King Cole’s attention; Cole’s 1948 recording became a hit and the song a standard.
Carmen — Bizet’s opera “Carmen” is based on Prosper Mérimée’s novella of the same name.
La traviata — Verdi’s “La traviata” is based on Alexandre Dumas fils’s play adapted from his novel “The Lady of the Camellias”.
Otello — Verdi’s “Otello”, with a libretto by Arrigo Boito, adapts Shakespeare’s tragedy “Othello”.
Eugene Onegin — Tchaikovsky’s opera “Eugene Onegin” is based on Alexander Pushkin’s verse novel and includes Tatiana’s letter scene and Lensky’s duel.
Wozzeck — Alban Berg’s opera “Wozzeck” adapts Georg Büchner’s unfinished drama “Woyzeck”.
Rodeo — Agnes de Mille choreographed “Rodeo” to music by Aaron Copland for the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo in 1942.
Appalachian Spring — Copland composed “Appalachian Spring” for Martha Graham; the title, taken from a Hart Crane poem, was selected after the music was written.
Billy the Kid — Lincoln Kirstein commissioned Copland’s ballet “Billy the Kid”, which uses American cowboy songs in its score.
Parade — The 1917 ballet “Parade” brought together Jean Cocteau, Erik Satie and Pablo Picasso for the Ballets Russes.
The Green Table — Kurt Jooss created the anti-war ballet “The Green Table” in 1932, framing its episodes with masked diplomats and the figure of Death.
Hunting High and Low — a-ha’s debut album “Hunting High and Low” includes the international hits “Take On Me” and “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.”.
The Sign — Ace of Base’s album “The Sign” adapted the earlier “Happy Nation” release for North America and became an international commercial success.

supportingSource.title: The Sign (Ace of Base album) — Wikipedia

assertion: Dead Letters — The Rasmus released “Dead Letters” in 2003; its single “In the Shadows” drove the Finnish band’s international breakthrough.
Homogenic — Björk shaped “Homogenic” around a contrast between string arrangements and electronic beats, linking its sound to Iceland.
Ágætis byrjun — Sigur Rós’s “Ágætis byrjun” became the Icelandic band’s international breakthrough and features Jónsi’s bowed-guitar sound.
Money — Pink Floyd’s “Money” opens with a rhythmic tape loop assembled from money-related sound effects.
Yellow Submarine — The Beatles and the Abbey Road staff added chains, bells, whistles, water sounds and other studio effects to “Yellow Submarine”.
The Typewriter — Leroy Anderson’s novelty piece “The Typewriter” uses a modified typewriter as a percussion instrument with orchestra.
Revolution 9 — The Beatles’ “Revolution 9” is a sound collage built from tape loops, spoken fragments, effects and reversed recordings.
My Life in the Bush of Ghosts — David Byrne and Brian Eno’s “My Life in the Bush of Ghosts” uses sampled voices from broadcasts and found recordings as central musical material.

supportingSource.title: My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (album) — Wikipedia

assertion: Y.M.C.A. — The disco hit inspired a crowd dance in which each letter of its title is shaped with the arms.
Macarena — The Bayside Boys remix helped turn the Spanish duo’s song and its accompanying routine into a worldwide craze.
Gangnam Style — Psy’s video made its comic horse-riding choreography globally recognisable and became the first YouTube video to reach one billion views.
The Twist — Checker’s version popularised both the song and the dance craze named in its title.
Saturday Night — Whigfield’s debut single became a European number-one hit and acquired a widely copied dance routine.
Despacito — The Puerto Rican artists’ song became a global hit in Spanish, with a later remix featuring Justin Bieber.
Dragostea Din Tei — The Moldovan group’s recording topped charts across Europe and supplied the refrain used in the viral “Numa Numa” video.
99 Luftballons — Nena’s anti-war song tells how balloons mistaken for a threat set off escalating military reactions; an English version was titled “99 Red Balloons”.
Rock Me Amadeus — The Austrian singer’s 1985 song about Mozart became the first German-language single to top the US Billboard Hot 100.
Alors on danse — The Belgian artist’s video follows a man from a hard day at work into a night of drinking and dancing.
Wish You Were Here — Hipgnosis used the burning handshake to evoke empty business dealings; the original LP was even shrink-wrapped without the band or album name.

supportingSource.title: Wish You Were Here | Pink Floyd Album

assertion: Ghostbusters — Ray Parker Jr. wrote and performed “Ghostbusters” as the theme song for the film of the same name.
I Will Always Love You — Whitney Houston recorded her arrangement of “I Will Always Love You” for the soundtrack to The Bodyguard.

supportingSource.title: I Will Always Love You — Wikipedia

assertion: Lose Yourself — “Lose Yourself” was written for 8 Mile and became the first hip-hop song to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
Gangsta’s Paradise — Coolio recorded “Gangsta’s Paradise” with singer L.V. for the Dangerous Minds soundtrack.
Born Slippy .NUXX — The film Trainspotting used Underworld’s “Born Slippy .NUXX” in its closing sequence, turning the track into a 1990s anthem.
ukulele — The ukulele developed in Hawaii from small Portuguese guitar-like instruments and commonly has four nylon strings.
steelpan — The steelpan was developed in Trinidad and Tobago and became a central instrument of its Carnival music.
marimba — A marimba uses wooden bars and resonator pipes, and its range extends lower than that of a xylophone.
bandoneon — The bandoneon is a button-operated free-reed instrument that became essential to tango in Argentina and Uruguay.
nyckelharpa — The Swedish nyckelharpa is bowed while wooden keys move tangents against its strings to select pitches.
celesta — A celesta looks like a small upright piano, but its keys operate hammers that strike metal plates; Tchaikovsky featured it in “Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy”.
ocarina — The ocarina is a vessel flute with an enclosed body and finger holes; The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time increased the instrument’s popularity and sales.
melodica — A melodica sends blown air across free reeds while its piano-style keys select the notes; Augustus Pablo popularised its use in reggae and dub.
musical saw — A musical saw is a flexible hand saw played with a bow; changing its curve alters the pitch and enables the continuous glissando often compared with a theremin.
glass harmonica — Franklin mechanised the sound of musical glasses by mounting graduated glass bowls on a rotating spindle, creating the glass harmonica or armonica.
flamenco — Flamenco developed in Andalusia and combines song, guitar playing and dance.
grunge — Grunge emerged around Seattle by combining punk and heavy-metal influences with a distorted guitar sound.
techno — Techno took shape in Detroit through producers including the Belleville Three, drawing on electronic music and house.
fado — Fado is a Portuguese song tradition strongly associated with Lisbon, Portuguese guitar and the feeling of saudade.
highlife — Highlife developed in Ghana from local musical traditions combined with brass-band, guitar and jazz influences.
waltz — The waltz is a rotating partner dance in triple metre that spread from German-speaking Europe.
polka — The polka originated in nineteenth-century Bohemia and is danced in a lively 2/4 metre.
samba — Samba grew from Afro-Brazilian traditions and became central to Carnival culture in Rio de Janeiro.
cha-cha-cha — The cha-cha-cha originated in Cuba, and its name imitates the sound of the dancers’ quick shuffling steps.
dabke — Dabke is a Levantine line or circle dance marked by rhythmic stamping and performed at celebrations.
Walk This Way — Run-DMC’s 1986 version brought Aerosmith into the recording and helped rap reach a wider rock audience.
Stan — Eminem’s narrative track samples Dido’s opening vocal and turns the fan’s name into the song’s central character.
Old Town Road — The Billy Ray Cyrus remix helped the country-rap track become a major crossover hit.
Barcelona — Mercury and Caballé recorded the title song for their joint album, and it became an anthem of the Barcelona Olympics.

supportingSource.title: Barcelona (Freddie Mercury and Montserrat Caballé song) — Wikipedia

assertion: Miss Sarajevo — The collaboration grew from Bill Carter’s documentary about a beauty pageant staged in besieged Sarajevo, with Pavarotti singing the operatic passage.
Girls Just Want to Have Fun — Hazard wrote and first recorded the song, while Lauper’s altered 1983 version became her breakthrough hit.

supportingSource.title: Girls Just Want to Have Fun — Wikipedia

assertion: Valerie — The Zutons released the original in 2006; Ronson’s 2007 cover featured Winehouse on vocals and reached number two in Britain.
Always on My Mind — The song had already produced major country and pop versions before Pet Shop Boys released their electronic remake in 1987.
The Man Who Sold the World — Bowie wrote and recorded the song in 1970; Nirvana’s 1993 acoustic performance became another widely known version.

supportingSource.title: The Man Who Sold the World (song) — Wikipedia

assertion: I Fought the Law — Curtis wrote the song for the Crickets; the Bobby Fuller Four and later the Clash made prominent cover versions.
Song 2 — The short, loud Blur single became widely used at sporting events and in sports media.
Mr. Brightside — Michigan Stadium made the chorus a crowd tradition at the end of the third quarter.
Sweet Caroline — Fenway Park regularly plays the song in the eighth inning, where its refrain has become a crowd ritual.
Kernkraft 400 — The Mariners began playing it during rallies in 2000, and fans chant along to its hook.
Three Lions — The song was recorded for UEFA Euro 1996 and became a recurring England-supporter anthem.
Space Oddity — Bowie’s story of the fictional astronaut Major Tom was released in July 1969, days before the Moon landing.
Rocket Man — Bernie Taupin’s lyrics describe an astronaut separated from his family, while Elton John wrote the music.
The Final Countdown — Joey Tempest wrote the famous keyboard riff that opens The Final Countdown.

assertion: Walking on the Moon — Sting’s lyrics use lunar gravity as a metaphor for love, while the band gives the song a sparse reggae-influenced arrangement.
Across the Universe — NASA selected the Beatles’ Across the Universe for a Deep Space Network transmission directed toward Polaris in February 2008.

supportingSource.title: NASA JPL: Beatles song beamed into deep space

assertion: Wind of Change — Klaus Meine wrote the song after the band’s experiences in the Soviet Union as political change swept Europe.
Candle in the Wind 1997 — Bernie Taupin replaced the original Marilyn Monroe lyrics with words honouring Diana; Elton John performed the new version at her funeral and it became a worldwide hit.
Beds Are Burning — The song criticises the removal of Aboriginal communities from their lands and repeats the demand to give the land back.
Ohio — Young wrote the song in immediate response to the May 1970 Kent State shootings.

supportingSource.title: Ohio (Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song) — Wikipedia

assertion: Hurricane — Dylan and Jacques Levy wrote the protest song about Carter’s case and imprisonment.
Careless Whisper — Gregory recorded the song’s prominent tenor-saxophone riff, which became its defining musical hook.
Paint It Black — Jones played sitar on the recording, adding the distinctive line above its driving rhythm.
Baker Street — Ravenscroft’s saxophone part became the best-known hook in Rafferty’s recording.
Baba O’Riley — Pete Townshend created the repeating keyboard pattern on a Lowrey organ, and Dave Arbus played the violin coda.
Golden Brown — The song is built around Greenfield’s harpsichord-led figure and an unusual pattern of three- and four-beat bars.
What a Wonderful World — The 1967 recording found a new audience when the 1987 film used it on its soundtrack.
Feeling Good — Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse wrote the song for the stage musical; Simone’s version became one of its best-known recordings.
Take the “A” Train — Strayhorn composed the tune from directions that began with taking New York’s A train, and it became Ellington’s orchestra theme.
My Baby Just Cares for Me — Simone recorded the standard in 1958; its use in a 1980s perfume advertisement brought the recording renewed chart success.

supportingSource.title: My Baby Just Cares for Me — Wikipedia

assertion: Birdland — Zawinul wrote the jazz-fusion standard for Weather Report and linked its title to the club named for Parker, known as “Bird”.
1812 Overture — Tchaikovsky’s 1812 Overture depicts the defeat of Napoleon’s invasion and famously calls for cannon fire and bells.
The Blue Danube — Johann Strauss II composed The Blue Danube, which premiered in Vienna in 1867 and became a classical favourite.
Nessun dorma — The BBC used Luciano Pavarotti’s recording of “Nessun dorma” as its theme for the 1990 FIFA World Cup.
Ride of the Valkyries — Apocalypse Now uses Wagner’s “Ride of the Valkyries” during its helicopter assault sequence.
O Fortuna — Carl Orff set the medieval Latin poem “O Fortuna” as the opening and closing movement of Carmina Burana.
Aida — Verdi’s Aida centres on an Ethiopian princess enslaved in Egypt and her forbidden love for Radamès.
The Barber of Seville — In Rossini’s The Barber of Seville, Figaro schemes to unite Count Almaviva with Rosina despite Bartolo’s plans.
Madama Butterfly — Puccini’s Madama Butterfly tells how Cio-Cio-San waits for Pinkerton, learns that he has returned with an American wife, and takes her own life.
Rigoletto — In Verdi’s Rigoletto, the jester discovers that the victim delivered in a sack is his daughter Gilda rather than the Duke.
The Tales of Hoffmann — Offenbach’s The Tales of Hoffmann builds its central acts around Hoffmann’s failed loves Olympia, Antonia and Giulietta.
The Sound of Music — The Sound of Music follows Maria as she becomes governess to the seven von Trapp children and falls in love with their father.
Hamilton — Hamilton is Lin-Manuel Miranda’s sung-and-rapped-through biographical musical about Alexander Hamilton.
Hairspray — Hairspray centres on Tracy Turnblad, a Baltimore teenager who joins a television dance show and challenges its segregation.
Wicked — Wicked retells events in Oz through the friendship and eventual rupture between Elphaba and Glinda.
Into the Woods — Into the Woods combines several Brothers Grimm fairy tales and explores what follows after their characters’ wishes come true.
Loreen — Loreen won Eurovision for Sweden with “Euphoria” in 2012 and again with “Tattoo” in 2023.
Verka Serduchka — Verka Serduchka represented Ukraine in 2007, and “Dancing Lasha Tumbai” finished second with 235 points.
Måns Zelmerlöw — Måns Zelmerlöw won both Melodifestivalen and Eurovision in 2015 with “Heroes”.
Salvador Sobral — Salvador Sobral won Eurovision 2017 with “Amar pelos dois”, ending Portugal’s 53-year wait for a first victory.
Johnny Logan — Johnny Logan won Eurovision as a performer in 1980 and 1987 and composed the winning song in 1992.
Anne Veski — “Roosiaia kuninganna” was Anne Veski’s first notable Estonian-language hit.
Ott Lepland — Ott Lepland won the third season of Eesti otsib superstaari and placed sixth at Eurovision 2012 with “Kuula”.
Lenna Kuurmaa — Lenna Kuurmaa was a member of Vanilla Ninja and released her debut solo album Lenna in 2010.
Urmas Alender — Urmas Alender fronted Ruja and Propeller and died when the ferry Estonia sank in 1994.
Jaak Joala — Jaak Joala became known as the “Kremlin’s Nightingale” after performing and recording widely in Russian.
I Wanna — Marie N performed the song with a choreographed costume transformation and gave Latvia its first Eurovision victory in 2002.
My Star — Brainstorm represented Latvia in the country’s first contest appearance and finished third with the song.
Sentimentai — The Lithuanian-language song represented Lithuania in Turin and qualified for the final.
We Are the Winners — LT United represented Lithuania with the song in 2006; the sixth-place finish was the country’s highest Eurovision placing at that time.
Love Injected — Aminata represented Latvia in 2015, qualified for the final and achieved the country’s strongest result in a decade.
Sandstorm — Darude’s 1999 instrumental became an international dance hit and later a recurring online and stadium reference.
Cotton Eye Joe — Rednex combined the traditional song with Eurodance and American instruments such as banjo and fiddle for an international hit.
Dancing on My Own — The Swedish singer’s electronic pop song places its narrator alone in a club, dancing while the former partner moves on.
The Look — A listener passed the album to station KDWB, whose airplay helped turn the song into Roxette’s first US number one.
It’s Oh So Quiet — Björk reworked a song previously recorded by Betty Hutton, and Jonze directed its exuberant musical-style video.
Hurt — Nine Inch Nails released “Hurt” in 1995; Cash covered it near the end of his life, and Trent Reznor praised the deeply personal reinterpretation.
Nothing Compares 2 U — Prince wrote “Nothing Compares 2 U” for the Family; O’Connor’s 1990 recording became her signature hit and its video centred on her face.
Hallelujah — Cohen released “Hallelujah” in 1984; Cale’s later arrangement inspired Buckley’s celebrated voice-and-guitar recording.
Killing Me Softly with His Song — “Killing Me Softly with His Song” was first recorded by Lieberman, then became a major hit for Flack and later for the Fugees.

supportingSource.title: Killing Me Softly with His Song — Wikipedia

assertion: All Along the Watchtower — Hendrix transformed Dylan’s “All Along the Watchtower” with layered guitars; Dylan later adopted elements of the cover in concert.
Shallow — “Shallow” is performed by Cooper and Gaga in A Star Is Born, moving from his opening lines to her climactic vocal.

supportingSource.title: Shallow (Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper song) — Wikipedia

assertion: Don’t Go Breaking My Heart — “Don’t Go Breaking My Heart” is an Elton John and Kiki Dee duet written as an affectionate pastiche of the Motown style.

supportingSource.title: Don't Go Breaking My Heart — Wikipedia

assertion: Empire State of Mind — “Empire State of Mind” pairs Jay-Z’s rap verses with Alicia Keys’s sung chorus as a tribute to New York City.
Don’t Give Up — In “Don’t Give Up”, Gabriel sings the despairing verses and Bush provides the encouraging response.

supportingSource.title: Don't Give Up (Peter Gabriel and Kate Bush song) — Wikipedia

assertion: Where the Wild Roses Grow — “Where the Wild Roses Grow” is a murder ballad whose alternating voices cast Cave as the killer and Minogue as Elisa Day, his victim.

supportingSource.title: Where the Wild Roses Grow — Wikipedia

assertion: The Wall — The Wall follows Pink as painful experiences become metaphorical bricks separating him from other people.
American Idiot — American Idiot is a rock opera centred on the antihero Jesus of Suburbia and his experiences in an alienating America.
The Black Parade — The Black Parade is a concept album about the Patient, a terminally ill man facing death and looking back on his life.

The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars — The album follows Ziggy Stardust from his arrival as a messenger through fame, an ego-driven loss of fans and bandmates, and a fall from grace.

supportingSource.title: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars — Wikipedia

assertion: Tommy — Tommy is the Who’s rock opera about Tommy Walker, whose extraordinary pinball skill leads to fame and a religious following.
(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction — The tape held about two minutes of acoustic guitar, then the sound of Richards dropping his pick and snoring for the next forty minutes.
Sweet Home Alabama — Ed King wrote and played the signature riff; the band wrote “Sweet Home Alabama” in response to Neil Young’s criticism of the American South.
Sweet Child o’ Mine — Sweet Child o’ Mine is built around Slash’s distinctive opening guitar riff.

supportingSource.title: Guitar World: How Slash’s riff became Sweet Child o’ Mine

assertion: Money for Nothing — Knopfler devised the “Money for Nothing” riff while improvising to a click track and modelled its guitar sound on Gibbons; Sting contributed the falsetto introduction.
Sunshine of Your Love — Bruce wrote the riff that anchors “Sunshine of Your Love” after seeing Hendrix perform in London in 1967.
Clocks — “Clocks” grew from Chris Martin’s repeating piano riff, which remains the song’s central musical idea.
Someone Like You — “Someone Like You” was written by Adele and Dan Wilson and recorded with Adele’s voice accompanied only by piano.
A Thousand Miles — “A Thousand Miles” opens with Carlton’s piano hook, and its music video famously shows her and the piano moving through several locations.
Your Song — “Your Song” was written by John and Taupin, appeared on Elton John and became John’s first international Top 10 single.
Great Balls of Fire — “Great Balls of Fire” was recorded by Lewis with Sidney Stokes on bass and Larry Linn on drums; Lewis supplied both piano and vocals.
Hollaback Girl — The Neptunes produced “Hollaback Girl” around a minimal programmed beat, while its cheerleading motif shapes the song’s shouted hook.
In the Air Tonight — The famous drum break in “In the Air Tonight” arrives towards the end and uses gated reverb, a sound strongly associated with 1980s pop.
Wipe Out — “Wipe Out” is built around Wilson’s energetic drum feature, one of surf rock’s best-known percussion passages.
When the Levee Breaks — For “When the Levee Breaks”, Bonham’s drums were recorded in a stairwell with distant microphones and heavy processing, producing their monumental sound.
Sing, Sing, Sing — Louis Prima wrote “Sing, Sing, Sing”; Benny Goodman’s recording became celebrated for Krupa’s unusually prominent extended drum solos.

supportingSource.title: Sing, Sing, Sing (with a Swing) — Wikipedia

assertion: Believe — “Believe” used extreme Auto-Tune settings as an audible effect, pioneering the vocal treatment often called the Cher effect.
Good Vibrations — “Good Vibrations” was constructed from many modular recording sessions across several studios, with its unusual electro-Theremin line helping define the sound.
Strawberry Fields Forever — “Strawberry Fields Forever” combines takes 7 and 26; varispeed brought their pitch and tempo close enough for a seamless edit.
Tomorrow Never Knows — “Tomorrow Never Knows” layers multiple tape loops and processes Lennon’s vocal through a Leslie speaker, making the studio central to the composition.
I Feel Love — The electronic pulse of “I Feel Love” was created with a Moog modular synthesiser and became highly influential on later dance music.
Auto-Tune — Auto-Tune analyses vocal pitch and shifts notes toward selected targets; fast correction produces its familiar stepped sound.
reverb — Reverb, short for reverberation, is the persistence of sound caused by reflections arriving after the original sound.
distortion — Distortion is the umbrella term for modification of a signal’s waveform; clipping and overdrive are common nonlinear forms used for guitar sounds.
vocoder — The vocoder was invented by Dudley at Bell Labs as a speech-synthesis and bandwidth-saving telecommunications system and was later widely used as an electronic musical instrument.
flanging — Flanging combines a sound with a slightly delayed, time-varying copy, causing moving peaks and notches in the frequency spectrum.
We Shall Overcome — “We Shall Overcome” grew from gospel and labour-song traditions and became the best-known anthem of the US civil-rights movement.
Blowin’ in the Wind — “Blowin’ in the Wind” poses rhetorical questions about war, peace and freedom; Peter, Paul and Mary helped turn it into a civil-rights standard.
Sunday Bloody Sunday — “Sunday Bloody Sunday” refers to Bloody Sunday in Derry and frames the conflict through an insistent martial rhythm while condemning violence.
Redemption Song — “Redemption Song” closes Marley’s Uprising album in a solo acoustic performance and adapts words from Marcus Garvey into a call for mental emancipation.
Biko — “Biko” tells of Steve Biko’s death in police custody and helped bring the anti-apartheid cause to a wider rock audience.
djembe — The djembe is a rope-tuned, skin-covered goblet drum from West Africa, played by hand with several distinct strokes.
bouzouki — The bouzouki is a long-necked Greek lute whose metallic sound became closely associated with rebetiko and modern Greek popular music.
koto — The koto is a Japanese long zither, commonly with thirteen strings stretched over movable bridges and plucked with picks.
erhu — The erhu is a two-stringed Chinese bowed instrument with a small soundbox traditionally covered in python skin.
kora — The kora is a 21-string West African bridge-harp traditionally played by griots, hereditary historians and musicians.
Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm — “Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm” uses a melody by Fredrik Pacius that is also used for Finland’s national anthem “Maamme”.

supportingSource.title: Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm — Wikipedia

assertion: La Marseillaise — “La Marseillaise” began in 1792 as a war song for the Army of the Rhine and took its familiar name from Marseille volunteers.
God Defend New Zealand — “God Defend New Zealand” is one of New Zealand’s two national anthems and has official lyrics in English and Māori.
Kimigayo — “Kimigayo” sets words based on a waka poem found in a tenth-century anthology, making its text far older than its modern melody.
March of the Volunteers — “March of the Volunteers” was created as the theme song of the 1935 film Children of Troubled Times before its adoption as China’s anthem.
Thriller — John Landis directed “Michael Jackson’s Thriller” as a horror short film whose central zombie dance became an enduring pop-culture image.
Sledgehammer — The “Sledgehammer” video used stop motion, clay animation and pixilation, requiring Gabriel to pose frame by frame.
This Is America — Hiro Murai directed “This Is America”, whose long tracking shots contrast viral dance choreography with abrupt violence and background disorder.
Here It Goes Again — OK Go’s “Here It Goes Again” video became famous for its choreographed one-take performance on treadmills.
Weapon of Choice — Spike Jonze directed the “Weapon of Choice” video, centred on Walken’s solo dance and flight through a Los Angeles hotel.
My Way — Paul Anka wrote English lyrics unrelated to the French words of “Comme d’habitude”; Frank Sinatra’s recording made “My Way” a standard.
The Lion Sleeps Tonight — “The Lion Sleeps Tonight” developed from Solomon Linda’s “Mbube”, which had also circulated internationally as “Wimoweh”.
Seasons in the Sun — Rod McKuen wrote the English adaptation “Seasons in the Sun” from Jacques Brel’s “Le Moribond”; Terry Jacks made it a major hit.
Beyond the Sea — “Beyond the Sea” uses the music of Charles Trenet’s “La Mer”, but Jack Lawrence’s English lyric is not a translation of the French words.
You Don’t Have to Say You Love Me — “You Don’t Have to Say You Love Me” is Dusty Springfield’s English adaptation of “Io che non vivo”; its English lyric is not a literal translation.

supportingSource.title: You Don't Have to Say You Love Me — Wikipedia

assertion: 21 — Adele wrote “21” in the aftermath of separation from a partner; its songs include “Rolling in the Deep” and “Someone Like You”.
Jagged Little Pill — “Jagged Little Pill” explores anger, broken relationships and recovery, including “You Oughta Know” and “Head over Feet”.
Blood on the Tracks — “Blood on the Tracks” has often been interpreted in relation to Bob Dylan’s marital turmoil, though Dylan disputed that straightforward reading.
Sea Change — Beck made “Sea Change” after his breakup with Leigh Limon, shaping its songs around melancholy acoustic arrangements and strings.
Here, My Dear — Marvin Gaye recorded “Here, My Dear” while divorcing Anna Gordy; the settlement tied proceeds from his next album to her.
Queen’s Live Aid performance — Queen played a widely celebrated set at Live Aid in Wembley Stadium on 13 July 1985, fronted by Freddie Mercury.
the Beatles’ rooftop concert — The Beatles performed unannounced on the roof of Apple Corps on 30 January 1969; it became their final public performance as a group.
the 1965 Newport Folk Festival — Bob Dylan’s amplified set at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival prompted controversy and became a landmark in his move toward electric rock.
the Concert for Bangladesh — George Harrison and Ravi Shankar organised the Concert for Bangladesh at Madison Square Garden in 1971 to aid refugees from the Bangladesh Liberation War.
The Last Waltz — The Last Waltz was the Band’s 1976 farewell concert, featuring many guests and filmed by Martin Scorsese.
Hung Up — Madonna’s “Hung Up” prominently samples the instrumental introduction to ABBA’s “Gimme! Gimme! Gimme! (A Man After Midnight)”.
Bitter Sweet Symphony — “Bitter Sweet Symphony” uses a sample from the Andrew Oldham Orchestra recording of “The Last Time”; its rights became the subject of a prolonged dispute.
Paper Planes — M.I.A.’s “Paper Planes” samples the Clash’s “Straight to Hell” and punctuates its chorus with gunshot and cash-register sounds.
Praise You — Fatboy Slim’s “Praise You” is built around a prominent sample of Camille Yarbrough’s “Take Yo’ Praise”.
Ready or Not — The Fugees’ “Ready or Not” samples Enya’s “Boadicea”; the unapproved use was later settled.
the iPod — Apple introduced the iPod in 2001 and promoted its capacity with the phrase “1,000 songs in your pocket”.
the compact disc — Philips and Sony collaborated on the compact disc, an optical digital-audio format commercially introduced in the early 1980s.
Napster — Napster launched as a peer-to-peer music-sharing service in 1999 and was forced to shut down after copyright litigation.
the transistor radio — The transistor radio used transistors instead of vacuum tubes, enabling small, battery-powered and portable receivers.
MiniDisc — Sony introduced MiniDisc in 1992 as a magneto-optical digital format positioned as a successor to the compact cassette.
Under Pressure — Queen and David Bowie wrote and recorded “Under Pressure” together after jamming at Mountain Studios in Switzerland.
Smooth — Santana’s “Smooth” features Rob Thomas as singer and co-writer and became a major 1999 chart hit.
Bring Me to Life — Evanescence’s “Bring Me to Life” pairs Amy Lee’s lead vocal with guest vocals from Paul McCoy of 12 Stones.
Numb/Encore — “Numb/Encore” combines Linkin Park’s “Numb” with Jay-Z’s “Encore” and appeared on their collaborative EP “Collision Course”.
Bring the Noise — Public Enemy and Anthrax released a joint 1991 version of “Bring the Noise”, influential in the development of rap metal.
Strange Fruit — Abel Meeropol wrote “Strange Fruit” as a protest against lynching; Billie Holiday’s recording made it famous.
Fortunate Son — “Fortunate Son” protests the unequal burden of the Vietnam War and the privilege enjoyed by politically connected families.
Free Nelson Mandela — Jerry Dammers wrote “Free Nelson Mandela”, recorded by the Special AKA in 1984 as an anti-apartheid protest.
Mississippi Goddam — Nina Simone wrote “Mississippi Goddam” in response to racist violence including Medgar Evers’s murder and the Birmingham church bombing.
Shipbuilding — “Shipbuilding”, with lyrics by Elvis Costello, reflects on shipyard jobs created by a war that also sends local men to fight; Robert Wyatt recorded an acclaimed version.
MTV Unplugged in New York — Nirvana’s “MTV Unplugged in New York” documents the band’s 1993 acoustic television performance, whose set avoided a conventional parade of hits.

supportingSource.title: MTV Unplugged in New York — Wikipedia

assertion: At Folsom Prison — Johnny Cash recorded “At Folsom Prison” before inmates at Folsom State Prison in January 1968.
Frampton Comes Alive! — Peter Frampton’s double live album “Frampton Comes Alive!” features hit live versions of “Show Me the Way” and “Do You Feel Like We Do”.
Live at Leeds — The Who recorded “Live at Leeds” at the University of Leeds Refectory on 14 February 1970.
Stop Making Sense — Jonathan Demme filmed Talking Heads for “Stop Making Sense”; its staged concert adds performers and equipment song by song and features David Byrne’s oversized suit.
Red Red Wine — Neil Diamond wrote and first recorded “Red Red Wine”; UB40’s reggae version became an international hit.
Twist and Shout — The Beatles recorded “Twist and Shout” in one take at the end of the session for their debut album, with John Lennon on lead vocal.
Black Magic Woman — Peter Green wrote “Black Magic Woman” for Fleetwood Mac; Santana’s hit recording combined it with Gábor Szabó’s “Gypsy Queen”.
The Tide Is High — The Paragons first recorded “The Tide Is High”; Blondie’s 1980 cover became a transatlantic number-one hit.
Me and Bobby McGee — Kris Kristofferson and Fred Foster wrote “Me and Bobby McGee”; Janis Joplin’s recording reached number one after her death.
the Monterey Pop Festival — Jimi Hendrix’s performance at the 1967 Monterey International Pop Festival, ending with his guitar being set on fire, helped establish him in the United States.
Rock in Rio — Queen played the first Rock in Rio in 1985, where the audience’s mass singalong to “Love of My Life” became one of the festival’s remembered images.

supportingSource.title: Love of My Life (Queen song) — Wikipedia

assertion: the Altamont Free Concert — At the 1969 Altamont Free Concert, Meredith Hunter was killed near the stage while the Hells Angels were acting as security.
the 1970 Isle of Wight Festival — The 1970 Isle of Wight Festival assembled those major acts at Afton Down and became one of the largest music events of its time.
the Harlem Cultural Festival — The 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival featured those performers; its long-unseen footage was presented in Questlove’s documentary “Summer of Soul”.
Roxanne — The opening of the Police’s “Roxanne” preserves an accidental piano chord and Sting’s laughter after he sat on the keyboard.
Like a Rolling Stone — Al Kooper, originally present as a guitarist, improvised the Hammond organ part heard on Bob Dylan’s “Like a Rolling Stone”.
You Really Got Me — Dave Davies produced the distorted guitar sound on “You Really Got Me” by cutting the speaker cone of his Elpico amplifier.
Gimme Shelter — Merry Clayton’s backing vocal on “Gimme Shelter” includes a voice crack, followed by an audible reaction from the studio.
In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida — Iron Butterfly’s title “In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida” arose when Ron Bushy transcribed Doug Ingle’s slurred pronunciation of “In the Garden of Eden”.
The Pink Panther Theme — Henry Mancini composed “The Pink Panther Theme” for the 1963 film; the tenor-saxophone-led recording became a successful single.
Gonna Fly Now — Bill Conti composed “Gonna Fly Now” as the training theme for the film “Rocky”; it later reached number one in the United States.
Lux Aeterna — Clint Mansell’s “Lux Aeterna” was written for “Requiem for a Dream”; an orchestral adaptation called “Requiem for a Tower” was used in “The Two Towers” advertising.

supportingSource.title: Lux Aeterna (Requiem for a Dream) — Wikipedia

assertion: The Ecstasy of Gold — Ennio Morricone composed “The Ecstasy of Gold” for “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly”; Metallica adopted it as concert entrance music.
Concerning Hobbits — Howard Shore’s “Concerning Hobbits” appears on “The Fellowship of the Ring” soundtrack and develops the Shire theme with folk-like instruments.
Rhapsody in Blue — George Gershwin composed “Rhapsody in Blue” for Paul Whiteman’s 1924 concert “An Experiment in Modern Music” and played the piano at its premiere.
the Eroica Symphony — Beethoven’s manuscript shows Napoleon’s name erased from the title page; the published work was titled “Sinfonia eroica”.
Water Music — Handel’s “Water Music” was performed for King George I during a royal barge journey on the Thames in 1717.
the Farewell Symphony — In the finale of Haydn’s Symphony No. 45, musicians leave one by one; the gesture is traditionally linked to their wish to return home from Esterháza.
Symphonie fantastique — Berlioz’s program for “Symphonie fantastique” follows an artist’s opium vision; its recurring idée fixe represents his beloved.
Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) — George Harrison played sitar on “Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)”, an early prominent use of the instrument on a Western rock recording.

supportingSource.title: Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) — Wikipedia

assertion: Penny Lane — Paul McCartney was inspired by the televised Bach performance to use piccolo trumpet in “Penny Lane”; George Martin arranged the part and David Mason performed it.
Mull of Kintyre — Wings recorded “Mull of Kintyre” with the Campbeltown Pipe Band, whose bagpipes are central to the arrangement.
Who Can It Be Now? — Men at Work’s “Who Can It Be Now?” features a prominent saxophone hook played by Greg Ham.

supportingSource.title: Who Can It Be Now? — Wikipedia

assertion: Going Up the Country — Canned Heat’s “Going Up the Country” adapts Henry Thomas’s “Bull Doze Blues”; Jim Horn plays its distinctive flute part.
Don’t Worry, Be Happy — Bobby McFerrin recorded “Don’t Worry, Be Happy” using only vocal and other sounds he made, without instruments; it became a US number one.

assertion: Blue Monday — New Order’s “Blue Monday” combined sequencers, synthesizers and electronic percussion and became the best-selling 12-inch single.
Autobahn — Kraftwerk’s album “Autobahn”, centred on its motorway-themed title track, brought the group international commercial success.
Oxygène — Jean-Michel Jarre recorded “Oxygène” in a home studio using analogue synthesizers and other electronic instruments.
Endtroducing..... — DJ Shadow’s “Endtroducing.....” was constructed almost entirely from samples and is recognised as a landmark of instrumental hip-hop.
Selected Ambient Works 85–92 — Aphex Twin’s debut album “Selected Ambient Works 85–92” collects tracks recorded by Richard D. James over several earlier years.
The Four Seasons — Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons” consists of four violin concertos accompanied by sonnets that describe scenes and weather in each season.
The Planets — Holst’s suite “The Planets” gives seven planets astrological characters, from Mars to Neptune, and does not include Earth.
Pictures at an Exhibition — Mussorgsky wrote Pictures at an Exhibition for solo piano; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration carries its gallery journey into the orchestra.

assertion: The Moldau — Smetana’s second “Má vlast” tone poem is “Vltava”, also known by the German name “The Moldau”, after the river that runs through Prague.
Scheherazade — Rimsky-Korsakov’s “Scheherazade” draws on “One Thousand and One Nights”, with a recurring solo violin associated with its storyteller.
